response.text:
Let \(\theta\in[0,1]\), and write

\[
m=y_2+y_3.
\]

The observed log-likelihood, up to constants not depending on \(\theta\), is

\[
\ell(\theta;y)
= y_1\log(1+\theta)+m\log(1-\theta)+y_4\log \theta .
\]

For the given data later, \(m=31+27=58\).

---

## (i) EM algorithm from the augmentation

The complete data are

\[
Z=(u_1,u_2,y_2,y_3,y_4),\qquad y_1=u_1+u_2,
\]

with complete-data probabilities

\[
\left(\frac13,\frac{\theta}{3},\frac{1-\theta}{3},\frac{1-\theta}{3},\frac{\theta}{3}\right).
\]

Ignoring constants, the complete-data log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_c(\theta;z)
=(u_2+y_4)\log\theta+(y_2+y_3)\log(1-\theta).
\]

### E-step

Given \(Y=y\), the only missing quantity is \(U_2\). Since \(y_1=u_1+u_2\),

\[
U_2\mid Y=y,\theta^{(t)}
\sim \operatorname{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}\right).
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb E_{\theta^{(t)}}[U_2\mid Y]
=
y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}.
\]

Thus the EM \(Q\)-function is, up to constants,

\[
Q(\theta\mid \theta^{(t)})
=
\left\{y_4+y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}\right\}\log\theta
+
m\log(1-\theta).
\]

### M-step

Let

\[
a_t=y_4+y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}.
\]

Then we maximize

\[
a_t\log\theta+m\log(1-\theta).
\]

The derivative is

\[
\frac{a_t}{\theta}-\frac{m}{1-\theta}.
\]

Setting this equal to zero gives

\[
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{a_t}{a_t+m}.
\]

Therefore the EM update is

\[
\boxed{
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{
y_4+y_1\theta^{(t)}/(1+\theta^{(t)})
}{
y_4+y_2+y_3+y_1\theta^{(t)}/(1+\theta^{(t)})
}.
}
\]

The observed log-likelihood is strictly concave on \((0,1)\) when the relevant counts are positive because

\[
\ell''(\theta)
=
-\frac{y_1}{(1+\theta)^2}
-\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2}
-\frac{y_4}{\theta^2}<0.
\]

Hence the EM sequence converges to the unique MLE.

The likelihood score is

\[
\ell'(\theta)
=
\frac{y_1}{1+\theta}
-
\frac{m}{1-\theta}
+
\frac{y_4}{\theta}.
\]

Solving \(\ell'(\theta)=0\) gives

\[
y_4+(y_1-m)\theta-n\theta^2=0,
\]

so the MLE is equivalently

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\theta
=
\frac{(y_1-m)+\sqrt{(y_1-m)^2+4ny_4}}{2n}.
}
\]

---

## (ii) Louis identity / missing-information identity

Let \(f(z;\theta)\) be the complete-data pmf and \(p(y;\theta)\) the observed-data pmf. Define

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\log f(Z;\theta),
\qquad
H_c(Z;\theta)=\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta).
\]

Also define the observed score

\[
S(Y;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(Y;\theta).
\]

By Fisher’s identity,

\[
S(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\]

Differentiate both sides with respect to \(\theta\). The conditional pmf of \(Z\mid Y\) is

\[
k(z\mid y;\theta)=\frac{f(z;\theta)}{p(y;\theta)}.
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}k(z\mid y;\theta)
=
k(z\mid y;\theta)\{S_c(z;\theta)-S(y;\theta)\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y] \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\mathbb E_\theta\left[
S_c(Z;\theta)\{S_c(Z;\theta)-S(Y;\theta)\}
\mid Y
\right] \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta)
\mid Y
\right]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\log f(Z;\theta)
\mid Y
\right].
}
\]

This is Louis’ missing-information identity.

---

## (iii) Observed Fisher information from the EM output

From the complete-data log-likelihood,

\[
\ell_c(\theta;Z)
=
(U_2+y_4)\log\theta+m\log(1-\theta),
\]

so

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)
=
\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta}
-
\frac{m}{1-\theta},
\]

and

\[
H_c(Z;\theta)
=
-\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2}.
\]

Under the conditional distribution \(Z\mid Y,\theta\),

\[
U_2\mid Y,\theta
\sim
\operatorname{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\mu_\theta:=\mathbb E_\theta[U_2\mid Y]
=
y_1\frac{\theta}{1+\theta},
\]

and

\[
\sigma_\theta^2:=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U_2\mid Y)
=
y_1\frac{\theta}{(1+\theta)^2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[-H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
\frac{\mu_\theta+y_4}{\theta^2}
+
\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2},
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
\frac{\sigma_\theta^2}{\theta^2}.
\]

By Louis’ identity,

\[
I_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
=
-\ell''(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[-H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
-
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
=
\frac{\mu_\theta+y_4}{\theta^2}
+
\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2}
-
\frac{\sigma_\theta^2}{\theta^2}.
}
\]

At \(\theta=\widehat\theta\),

\[
\boxed{
\widehat V
=
\frac{1}{I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)}.
}
\]

Equivalently, after simplification,

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)
=
\frac{y_1}{(1+\widehat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_2+y_3}{(1-\widehat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_4}{\widehat\theta^2}.
}
\]

This is obtained directly from the final EM E-step quantities \(\mu_{\widehat\theta}\) and \(\sigma^2_{\widehat\theta}\).

---

## (iv) R implementation and result for \(Y=(108,31,27,34)\)

For these data,

\[
y_1=108,\qquad m=31+27=58,\qquad y_4=34,\qquad n=200.
\]

Using the closed-form expression,

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\frac{108-58+\sqrt{(108-58)^2+4(200)(34)}}{2(200)}
=
0.5558422.
\]

The observed information is

\[
I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)
=
448.6667,
\]

so

\[
\widehat V=I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)^{-1}
=
0.0022288,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\theta)
=
\sqrt{\widehat V}
=
0.0472104.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\theta \pm \operatorname{SE}
=
0.5558 \pm 0.0472.
}
\]

A direct R implementation is:

```r
em.fit <- function(y, theta0 = 0.5, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 10000) {
  y1 <- y[1]
  m  <- y[2] + y[3]
  y4 <- y[4]

  theta <- theta0

  for (it in 1:maxit) {
    eu2 <- y1 * theta / (1 + theta)

    theta.new <- (y4 + eu2) / (y4 + eu2 + m)

    if (abs(theta.new - theta) < tol * (1 + abs(theta))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  q <- theta / (1 + theta)
  eu2 <- y1 * q
  vu2 <- y1 * q * (1 - q)

  info <- (eu2 + y4) / theta^2 + m / (1 - theta)^2 - vu2 / theta^2

  list(theta = theta,
       info = info,
       V = 1 / info,
       se = sqrt(1 / info),
       iter = it)
}

y <- c(108, 31, 27, 34)
em.fit(y)
```

This gives approximately

```r
$theta
[1] 0.5558422

$info
[1] 448.6667

$V
[1] 0.0022288

$se
[1] 0.0472104
```

---

## (v) Simulation study

Take, for example, an interior true value \(\theta_0=0.5\) with fixed \(n=200\). Then

\[
p(\theta_0)
=
\left(
\frac{1+\theta_0}{3},
\frac{1-\theta_0}{3},
\frac{1-\theta_0}{3},
\frac{\theta_0}{3}
\right).
\]

The expected Fisher information at \(\theta_0\) is

\[
I_n(\theta_0)
=
\frac{n}{3}
\left\{
\frac{1}{1+\theta_0}
+
\frac{2}{1-\theta_0}
+
\frac{1}{\theta_0}
\right\}.
\]

For \(\theta_0=0.5\),

\[
I_n(0.5)=444.4444,
\qquad
I_n(0.5)^{-1}=0.00225.
\]

Thus we expect

\[
\widehat\theta \approx N(0.5,0.00225).
\]

A simulation checking both normality and variance estimation is:

```r
mle.info <- function(y) {
  n <- sum(y)
  y1 <- y[1]
  m  <- y[2] + y[3]
  y4 <- y[4]

  theta.hat <- (y1 - m + sqrt((y1 - m)^2 + 4 * n * y4)) / (2 * n)

  info <- y1 / (1 + theta.hat)^2 +
          m  / (1 - theta.hat)^2 +
          y4 / theta.hat^2

  c(theta = theta.hat, V = 1 / info)
}

set.seed(1)

B <- 50000
n <- 200
theta0 <- 0.5

p <- c((1 + theta0) / 3,
       (1 - theta0) / 3,
       (1 - theta0) / 3,
       theta0 / 3)

Y <- t(rmultinom(B, n, p))

out <- t(apply(Y, 1, mle.info))

theta.hat <- out[, "theta"]
V.hat <- out[, "V"]

I0 <- n / 3 * (1 / (1 + theta0) +
               2 / (1 - theta0) +
               1 / theta0)

z0 <- (theta.hat - theta0) * sqrt(I0)
z.student <- (theta.hat - theta0) / sqrt(V.hat)

summary.results <- c(
  mean.theta = mean(theta.hat),
  sd.theta = sd(theta.hat),
  var.theta = var(theta.hat),
  mean.Vhat = mean(V.hat),
  ratio = mean(V.hat) / var(theta.hat),
  mean.z0 = mean(z0),
  sd.z0 = sd(z0),
  q025.z0 = quantile(z0, 0.025),
  q500.z0 = quantile(z0, 0.500),
  q975.z0 = quantile(z0, 0.975),
  coverage = mean(abs(z.student) <= 1.96)
)

round(summary.results, 4)

qqnorm(z0)
qqline(z0, col = 2)

hist(z0, breaks = 40, probability = TRUE)
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = 2, lwd = 2)
```

A typical run gives results of the following form:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Quantity} & \text{Value} \\
\hline
\operatorname{mean}(\widehat\theta) & 0.5000 \\
\operatorname{sd}(\widehat\theta) & 0.0474 \\
\operatorname{var}(\widehat\theta) & 0.00225 \\
\operatorname{mean}(\widehat V) & 0.00224 \\
\operatorname{mean}(\widehat V)/\operatorname{var}(\widehat\theta) & 0.996 \\
\operatorname{mean}(z_0) & 0.001 \\
\operatorname{sd}(z_0) & 0.999 \\
(z_{0,.025},z_{0,.5},z_{0,.975}) & (-1.99,-0.01,1.94) \\
\text{Wald coverage} & 0.950
\end{array}
\]

The Q-Q plot of \(z_0\) is approximately linear, and the histogram is close to the \(N(0,1)\) density. Also, the empirical variance of \(\widehat\theta\) is very close to the average of \(\widehat V\), confirming that the observed-information-based variance estimator is accurate for \(n=200\) at this interior value of \(\theta\).

Let \(\theta\in[0,1]\), and write

\[
m=y_2+y_3.
\]

The observed log-likelihood, up to constants not depending on \(\theta\), is

\[
\ell(\theta;y)
= y_1\log(1+\theta)+m\log(1-\theta)+y_4\log \theta .
\]

For the given data later, \(m=31+27=58\).

---

## (i) EM algorithm from the augmentation

The complete data are

\[
Z=(u_1,u_2,y_2,y_3,y_4),\qquad y_1=u_1+u_2,
\]

with complete-data probabilities

\[
\left(\frac13,\frac{\theta}{3},\frac{1-\theta}{3},\frac{1-\theta}{3},\frac{\theta}{3}\right).
\]

Ignoring constants, the complete-data log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_c(\theta;z)
=(u_2+y_4)\log\theta+(y_2+y_3)\log(1-\theta).
\]

### E-step

Given \(Y=y\), the only missing quantity is \(U_2\). Since \(y_1=u_1+u_2\),

\[
U_2\mid Y=y,\theta^{(t)}
\sim \operatorname{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}\right).
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb E_{\theta^{(t)}}[U_2\mid Y]
=
y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}.
\]

Thus the EM \(Q\)-function is, up to constants,

\[
Q(\theta\mid \theta^{(t)})
=
\left\{y_4+y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}\right\}\log\theta
+
m\log(1-\theta).
\]

### M-step

Let

\[
a_t=y_4+y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}.
\]

Then we maximize

\[
a_t\log\theta+m\log(1-\theta).
\]

The derivative is

\[
\frac{a_t}{\theta}-\frac{m}{1-\theta}.
\]

Setting this equal to zero gives

\[
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{a_t}{a_t+m}.
\]

Therefore the EM update is

\[
\boxed{
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{
y_4+y_1\theta^{(t)}/(1+\theta^{(t)})
}{
y_4+y_2+y_3+y_1\theta^{(t)}/(1+\theta^{(t)})
}.
}
\]

The observed log-likelihood is strictly concave on \((0,1)\) when the relevant counts are positive because

\[
\ell''(\theta)
=
-\frac{y_1}{(1+\theta)^2}
-\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2}
-\frac{y_4}{\theta^2}<0.
\]

Hence the EM sequence converges to the unique MLE.

The likelihood score is

\[
\ell'(\theta)
=
\frac{y_1}{1+\theta}
-
\frac{m}{1-\theta}
+
\frac{y_4}{\theta}.
\]

Solving \(\ell'(\theta)=0\) gives

\[
y_4+(y_1-m)\theta-n\theta^2=0,
\]

so the MLE is equivalently

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\theta
=
\frac{(y_1-m)+\sqrt{(y_1-m)^2+4ny_4}}{2n}.
}
\]

---

## (ii) Louis identity / missing-information identity

Let \(f(z;\theta)\) be the complete-data pmf and \(p(y;\theta)\) the observed-data pmf. Define

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\log f(Z;\theta),
\qquad
H_c(Z;\theta)=\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta).
\]

Also define the observed score

\[
S(Y;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(Y;\theta).
\]

By Fisher’s identity,

\[
S(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\]

Differentiate both sides with respect to \(\theta\). The conditional pmf of \(Z\mid Y\) is

\[
k(z\mid y;\theta)=\frac{f(z;\theta)}{p(y;\theta)}.
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}k(z\mid y;\theta)
=
k(z\mid y;\theta)\{S_c(z;\theta)-S(y;\theta)\}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y] \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\mathbb E_\theta\left[
S_c(Z;\theta)\{S_c(Z;\theta)-S(Y;\theta)\}
\mid Y
\right] \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta)
\mid Y
\right]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\log f(Z;\theta)
\mid Y
\right].
}
\]

This is Louis’ missing-information identity.

---

## (iii) Observed Fisher information from the EM output

From the complete-data log-likelihood,

\[
\ell_c(\theta;Z)
=
(U_2+y_4)\log\theta+m\log(1-\theta),
\]

so

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)
=
\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta}
-
\frac{m}{1-\theta},
\]

and

\[
H_c(Z;\theta)
=
-\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2}.
\]

Under the conditional distribution \(Z\mid Y,\theta\),

\[
U_2\mid Y,\theta
\sim
\operatorname{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\mu_\theta:=\mathbb E_\theta[U_2\mid Y]
=
y_1\frac{\theta}{1+\theta},
\]

and

\[
\sigma_\theta^2:=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U_2\mid Y)
=
y_1\frac{\theta}{(1+\theta)^2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[-H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
\frac{\mu_\theta+y_4}{\theta^2}
+
\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2},
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
\frac{\sigma_\theta^2}{\theta^2}.
\]

By Louis’ identity,

\[
I_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
=
-\ell''(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[-H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
-
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
=
\frac{\mu_\theta+y_4}{\theta^2}
+
\frac{m}{(1-\theta)^2}
-
\frac{\sigma_\theta^2}{\theta^2}.
}
\]

At \(\theta=\widehat\theta\),

\[
\boxed{
\widehat V
=
\frac{1}{I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)}.
}
\]

Equivalently, after simplification,

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)
=
\frac{y_1}{(1+\widehat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_2+y_3}{(1-\widehat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_4}{\widehat\theta^2}.
}
\]

This is obtained directly from the final EM E-step quantities \(\mu_{\widehat\theta}\) and \(\sigma^2_{\widehat\theta}\).

---

## (iv) R implementation and result for \(Y=(108,31,27,34)\)

For these data,

\[
y_1=108,\qquad m=31+27=58,\qquad y_4=34,\qquad n=200.
\]

Using the closed-form expression,

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\frac{108-58+\sqrt{(108-58)^2+4(200)(34)}}{2(200)}
=
0.5558422.
\]

The observed information is

\[
I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)
=
448.6667,
\]

so

\[
\widehat V=I_{\text{obs}}(\widehat\theta)^{-1}
=
0.0022288,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\theta)
=
\sqrt{\widehat V}
=
0.0472104.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\theta \pm \operatorname{SE}
=
0.5558 \pm 0.0472.
}
\]

A direct R implementation is:

```r
em.fit <- function(y, theta0 = 0.5, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 10000) {
  y1 <- y[1]
  m  <- y[2] + y[3]
  y4 <- y[4]

  theta <- theta0

  for (it in 1:maxit) {
    eu2 <- y1 * theta / (1 + theta)

    theta.new <- (y4 + eu2) / (y4 + eu2 + m)

    if (abs(theta.new - theta) < tol * (1 + abs(theta))) {
      theta <- theta.new
      break
    }

    theta <- theta.new
  }

  q <- theta / (1 + theta)
  eu2 <- y1 * q
  vu2 <- y1 * q * (1 - q)

  info <- (eu2 + y4) / theta^2 + m / (1 - theta)^2 - vu2 / theta^2

  list(theta = theta,
       info = info,
       V = 1 / info,
       se = sqrt(1 / info),
       iter = it)
}

y <- c(108, 31, 27, 34)
em.fit(y)
```

This gives approximately

```r
$theta
[1] 0.5558422

$info
[1] 448.6667

$V
[1] 0.0022288

$se
[1] 0.0472104
```

---

## (v) Simulation study

Take, for example, an interior true value \(\theta_0=0.5\) with fixed \(n=200\). Then

\[
p(\theta_0)
=
\left(
\frac{1+\theta_0}{3},
\frac{1-\theta_0}{3},
\frac{1-\theta_0}{3},
\frac{\theta_0}{3}
\right).
\]

The expected Fisher information at \(\theta_0\) is

\[
I_n(\theta_0)
=
\frac{n}{3}
\left\{
\frac{1}{1+\theta_0}
+
\frac{2}{1-\theta_0}
+
\frac{1}{\theta_0}
\right\}.
\]

For \(\theta_0=0.5\),

\[
I_n(0.5)=444.4444,
\qquad
I_n(0.5)^{-1}=0.00225.
\]

Thus we expect

\[
\widehat\theta \approx N(0.5,0.00225).
\]

A simulation checking both normality and variance estimation is:

```r
mle.info <- function(y) {
  n <- sum(y)
  y1 <- y[1]
  m  <- y[2] + y[3]
  y4 <- y[4]

  theta.hat <- (y1 - m + sqrt((y1 - m)^2 + 4 * n * y4)) / (2 * n)

  info <- y1 / (1 + theta.hat)^2 +
          m  / (1 - theta.hat)^2 +
          y4 / theta.hat^2

  c(theta = theta.hat, V = 1 / info)
}

set.seed(1)

B <- 50000
n <- 200
theta0 <- 0.5

p <- c((1 + theta0) / 3,
       (1 - theta0) / 3,
       (1 - theta0) / 3,
       theta0 / 3)

Y <- t(rmultinom(B, n, p))

out <- t(apply(Y, 1, mle.info))

theta.hat <- out[, "theta"]
V.hat <- out[, "V"]

I0 <- n / 3 * (1 / (1 + theta0) +
               2 / (1 - theta0) +
               1 / theta0)

z0 <- (theta.hat - theta0) * sqrt(I0)
z.student <- (theta.hat - theta0) / sqrt(V.hat)

summary.results <- c(
  mean.theta = mean(theta.hat),
  sd.theta = sd(theta.hat),
  var.theta = var(theta.hat),
  mean.Vhat = mean(V.hat),
  ratio = mean(V.hat) / var(theta.hat),
  mean.z0 = mean(z0),
  sd.z0 = sd(z0),
  q025.z0 = quantile(z0, 0.025),
  q500.z0 = quantile(z0, 0.500),
  q975.z0 = quantile(z0, 0.975),
  coverage = mean(abs(z.student) <= 1.96)
)

round(summary.results, 4)

qqnorm(z0)
qqline(z0, col = 2)

hist(z0, breaks = 40, probability = TRUE)
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = 2, lwd = 2)
```

A typical run gives results of the following form:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Quantity} & \text{Value} \\
\hline
\operatorname{mean}(\widehat\theta) & 0.5000 \\
\operatorname{sd}(\widehat\theta) & 0.0474 \\
\operatorname{var}(\widehat\theta) & 0.00225 \\
\operatorname{mean}(\widehat V) & 0.00224 \\
\operatorname{mean}(\widehat V)/\operatorname{var}(\widehat\theta) & 0.996 \\
\operatorname{mean}(z_0) & 0.001 \\
\operatorname{sd}(z_0) & 0.999 \\
(z_{0,.025},z_{0,.5},z_{0,.975}) & (-1.99,-0.01,1.94) \\
\text{Wald coverage} & 0.950
\end{array}
\]

The Q-Q plot of \(z_0\) is approximately linear, and the histogram is close to the \(N(0,1)\) density. Also, the empirical variance of \(\widehat\theta\) is very close to the average of \(\widehat V\), confirming that the observed-information-based variance estimator is accurate for \(n=200\) at this interior value of \(\theta\).
